appraisal_events.evidence: « intimidé comme un collégien qui entre pour la première fois dans une maison publique » ; « On aurait cru voir s'avancer Mme de Marsantes, tant ressortait à ce moment la femme qu'une erreur de la nature avait mise dans le corps de M. de Charlus » ; « ce corps [...] déploya, au point que le baron eût mérité l'épithète de lady-like, toutes les séductions d'une grande dame ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator turns Charlus's entrance into a sustained comic anatomy in which the involuntary woman in him defeats the virile self-presentation he labors to maintain, extending the exposure to his self-deception and to the petty, offended froideur he displays toward Cottard. The diminishment is delivered through irony and analogy (the timid painter, Mme Cottard's nephew) rather than direct condemnation.

appraisal_events.evidence: « son nez avait choisi [...] la seule ligne oblique [...] qui signifiait une bêtise vulgaire » ; « le nez est généralement l'organe où s'étale le plus aisément la bêtise » ; at table « le marquis, lequel confessait sa bêtise » while Cottard demolishes his ready-made phrases and Mme Verdurin answers him with « cette acerbe riposte ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's physiognomic portrait fixes the marquis as vulgarly stupid and explicitly overrides the admiring provincial verdict of the première présidente, and the dinner then stages that verdict socially through his low bow to Brichot, his confessed ignorance, Cottard's corrections, and his wife's severe glance at his self-abasement.

status_effects.explanation: Charlus is locally lowered because the passage systematically exposes the gap between the grand seigneur he means to display and the timid, mincing, self-deceived figure the narrator describes.

Within the same entrance scene his social value in this salon rises: Mme Verdurin parades « le baron », Cottard is incredulous at finding one present, and Mme de Cambremer's whole mood changes at the chance of meeting at last « cet homme inapprochable » — a gain qualified by M. Verdurin ranking him below the marquis for precedence.
The marquis is clearly diminished: his face is read as an advertisement of stupidity, and at table he is corrected, mocked, and made to confess his ignorance before the fidèles.

ambiguities: Charlus's local movement is genuinely two-directional: the narrator's ironizing anatomy diminishes him while the salon treats him as a coveted, hard-to-approach baron; the annotation commits to narrator-led diminishment as dominant and records the countervailing social gain as a secondary, lower-confidence effect.

The narrator's stance on Charlus's femininity is unstable between endorsed analysis (asserted as a law of inversion) and comic staging (« lady-like », the invisible manchon, Mme Cottard's nephew); read here as ironized, which softens the diminishment from a moral verdict into an exposure.
